title: Tibetans
capsule: Following the fragmentation of the Tibetan Empire in the mid-9th century, Tibet's plateau dissolved into competing monastic and noble fiefs for roughly four centuries without a unified state; the period 850–1259 in the dataset reflects the presence of Tibetan-speaking polities on the plateau exercising local authority. Major religious schools — the Kadampa, Kagyupa, and Sakyapa — accumulated territorial power, and the Sakya school rose to paramountcy as Mongol patrons under Godan Khan and Kublai Khan formalized Sakya rule over Tibet c. 1244–1253, effectively ending the era of fragmented Tibetan autonomy and incorporating the plateau into the Mongol imperial system by 1253.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The geometry for this period is highly conjectural; no administrative records defining plateau-wide Tibetan territorial control survive from this fragmented interval, and the extent is inferred from the distribution of Buddhist monastic foundations and Chinese dynastic accounts.
